KEY MESSAGE 1...Today still looks to be largely dry, but cannot 
completely rule out an isolated shower or storm this afternoon and 
early evening. Daily chances for showers and thunderstorms will 
return Monday and into the middle of the week. There is a risk for 
strong to severe thunderstorms during the week, as well as a 
marginal risk for localized heavy rainfall leading to flash flooding.

A weak cold front has been passing through the area today which will 
continue to usher in slightly drier air. This combined with subtle 
subsidence and rising heights aloft will continue to limit the 
convection potential today. However, we cannot completely rule out 
some isolated convection popping up through early this evening, 
especially along the sea and/or bay bay breezes. These will act as 
surface forcing mechanisms where the westerly surface winds inland 
meet the southerly surface winds over the marine areas. If anything 
does develop, it'll be battling several limiting factors such as dry 
air aloft and subsidence, and will be short lived as shear is 
generally less than 20 kts. DCAPE and low-level lapse rates are high 
though, so any stronger storms could produce brief strong wind gusts 
and frequent lightning. Convective potential will end by sunset as 
today's activity would be diurnally driven.

A mid-level shortwave trough will approach the area Monday afternoon 
into the evening as mean flow shifts more westerly and mid-level 
flow increases amid falling heights. The timing of this synoptic 
evolution has continued to be a bit earlier with the recent guidance 
for Monday. This mid-level shortwave trough will be moving in from 
the west which means it will initiate showers and thunderstorms off 
to our west Monday morning. Currently, model guidance decays this 
activity before it reaches our area and keeps it off to the west. 
Monday's convection potential will at least partially depend on
what occurs upstream of our area through the day. 

For this update, SPC has maintained the Marginal (level 1 out of 5) 
Risk for severe thunderstorms for much of our forecast area for
Monday. The Slight (level 2 out of 5) Risk was expanded east 
today right to our forecast area border. There remains 
uncertainty around tomorrow, but an additional expansion further
east into our forecast area is possible if trends continue to 
hold. Given the recent trends among CAM guidance and model 
soundings, the primary risk is damaging wind gusts as there 
looks to be more of an upscale growth potential into a line 
segment as the activity approaches our area. Instability and 
low-level lapse rates are supportive of severe weather along 
with increasing bulk shear values for storm organization. 
Another note, there could also be a non-zero tornado threat as 
well as model guidance shows low- level shear increasing during 
the afternoon and evening. However, there remains a bit of 
uncertainty around how some of thermodynamics evolve through 
tomorrow afternoon and evening. 

In terms of flash flooding, there is a Marginal (level 1 out 4) Risk 
for excessive rainfall for areas mainly near and northwest of the I-
95 corridor. PWATs do look to increase again to upwards of 2 inches, 
so there is the heavy rain potential. However, with a more linear 
storm mode being possible, this will lead to a more progressive 
storm motion as the mid-level flow increases tomorrow. One takeaway 
with this forecast update is there remains uncertainty around the 
timing of the convection. Variations remain among model guidance and 
what happens for our forecast area will also depend on what happens 
upstream to our north and west with that convective development.

Recent forecast trends have resulted in lower instability compared 
to previous runs on Tuesday given the faster evolution of the 
synoptic features (cold front and shortwave trough).
Essentially, it looks like Tuesday's activity will be shunted to our 
southwest compared to previous forecasts based on the latest 
synoptic trends. With that said, we could still see some convection 
potential or even get the remnants of whatever occurs upstream later 
in the evening. So while the threat of severe storms now appears to 
be lessening for Tuesday, we could still get showers and storms in 
some form. Details for Tuesday are even more uncertain than Monday, 
and Monday's activity will probably play some role in what exactly 
happens Tuesday.

A cold front looks to stall to our northwest Tuesday into 
Wednesday. Multiple waves look to ride along the stalled
boundary which will support diurnally driven convection
continuing at least through Thursday. The front looks to push 
through by late Thursday and a much drier and cooler airmass 
will arrive by Friday and Saturday as a result, which will bring
us a more pronounced break in convective potential and more 
pleasant weather conditions.
